props.title: Voodoo Man
props.initialSlug: Mad doctor kidnaps brides for voodoo ritual

sections.content: Voodoo Man (1944) represents one of Bela Lugosi's fascinating later-career horror entries, joining his string of Monogram Pictures B-movies that included Bowery at Midnight (1942) and The Corpse Vanishes (1942). This poverty row production follows Dr. Richard Marlowe (Lugosi) kidnapping young women to perform voodoo rituals in an attempt to resurrect his dead wife. The film's lean 62-minute runtime exemplifies the efficient B-movie formula of the 1940s, when horror films often served as second features on double bills. Despite its low budget, it manages to create an effectively creepy atmosphere through Lugosi's commanding presence.

sections.content: The voodoo horror subgenre reached its early peak with White Zombie (1932), which established many tropes that Voodoo Man would later draw from. Producer Val Lewton elevated the subject matter with I Walked with a Zombie (1943), bringing sophisticated psychological horror to what had largely been exploitation territory. These films reflected America's simultaneous fascination with and fear of Caribbean spiritual practices, often problematically conflating various African-derived religions into a single mysterious "other." SUBHEAD: Bela Lugosi's Later Career

Voodoo Man came at a crucial point in Lugosi's career trajectory, following his iconic role in Dracula (1931). While still commanding attention on screen, he was increasingly relegated to smaller productions like The Devil Bat (1940) and Black Dragons (1942). These Monogram pictures, while considered lesser works, allowed Lugosi to continue crafting memorable performances even as major studio roles became scarce. His portrayal of Dr. Marlowe contains echoes of his earlier sophistication while embracing the more direct menace these quickie productions demanded.
